title: What Patients Think of AI-Assisted Health Care Communication

summary: Pediatric health care systems face increasing uncertainty driven by rapid technological change, workforce shifts and shortages, environmental threats, and evolving family and community needs. Pediatrics requires future-focused considerations that go beyond adult systems, including family-centered care, developmental trajectories, and long-term societal impacts on child well-being. While the future cannot be predicted, futures medicine methods offer structured approaches to anticipate change and support proactive, values-driven planning. This Viewpoint describes the application of pediatric futures methods within an academic, independent nonprofit pediatric health system and proposes a practical framework that connects future readiness to strategic decision-making and daily care delivery. Futures medicine methods are not new in pediatric health care but may not be visible from the front line of care delivery, which provides an opportunity for clinical, operational, administrative, and enterprise leaders to implement these methods in their workflows. This paper introduces the discover to deliver pediatric futures framework, a continuum that links long-range futures discovery to near-term strategic planning, operational design, implementation, and outcome demonstration, emphasizing future methods and activities for applicable use.
title: Discover to Deliver Pediatric Futures: Viewpoints of Future Medicine From a Pediatric Health Care System

summary: Background: Voice disorders are common, yet access to timely specialist assessment is often limited. Automated analysis of short voice recordings may support early screening, but achieving robust performance on heterogeneous clinical datasets remains challenging. Objective: This study aims to investigate the impact of synthetic speech augmentation on voice disorder recognition and classification using the Saarbrücken Voice Database (SVD) and to develop an adaptive ensemble with learnable weighting and optional sex embedding. Methods: Sentence recordings from the SVD were used for binary voice disorder recognition (VDR, n=1988) and 4-class voice disorder classification (VDC; n=1199). Two text-to-speech (TTS) models, XTTS and Kartoffelbox, generated 1 synthetic sample for each training instance. Synthetic speech quality was assessed in a blinded listening evaluation with 40 samples per TTS model. Baseline models included support vector machine (SVM), ResNet-18, long short-term memory, and transformer-based architectures, including Hidden-Unit BERT (HuBERT), Wav2Vec 2.0, and WavLM. Ensemble learning and learnable fusion (LF), with and without a sex embedding (LFS), were evaluated using bootstrapped performance estimates and standard classification metrics. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was reported for VDR. Results: In the blinded evaluation, Kartoffelbox-generated synthetic samples were less often identified as synthetic than XTTS-generated synthetic samples (10/19, 52.6% vs 17/19, 89.5%). In pooled original and synthetic ratings, Kartoffelbox showed higher pathological-status identification than XTTS for pathological samples (22/29, 75.9% vs 19/29, 65.5%) and nonpathological samples (8/10, 80.0% vs 6/10, 60.0%), as well as higher diagnostic-class assignment (20/39, 51.3% vs 14/39, 35.9%). Among the baseline models, HuBERT showed the most balanced VDR performance (accuracy=0.85, -score=0.84). Kartoffelbox-based augmentation further improved performance, with HuBERT achieving 0.88 sensitivity, 0.87 accuracy, and 0.85 -score. LF showed minor improvements in threshold-dependent metrics (accuracy=0.87, -score=0.86), while LFS further balanced sensitivity and specificity (accuracy=0.88, AUC=0.92). The equal-weight ensemble achieved the highest AUC among ensemble approaches (AUC=0.93). For VDC, HuBERT was the strongest baseline (accuracy=0.72, median -score=0.63), and LF achieved the highest overall fusion performance (accuracy=0.73, -score=0.66), while laryngitis remained one of the more challenging classes. Conclusions: High-quality synthetic speech augmentation can improve automated voice disorder analysis across heterogeneous clinical data, with effectiveness varying by the TTS model. Multimodel fusion of complementary architectures provided robust performance for screening and multiclass classification, with the strongest approach varying by metric and task. These findings support further evaluation of AI-assisted preassessment in clinical and telemedicine settings.
title: Detection of Pathological Voice Samples Using a Text-to-Speech–Inspired Approach With Multiple Model Architectures: Method Development and Comparative Evaluation Study

summary: Background: AI-based clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSSs) can help primary care clinicians provide higher quality care amid rising case complexity and resource constraints. However, evidence regarding their effectiveness and safety in primary care practice is lacking. Objective: We synthesized evidence on the effectiveness and safety of AI-CDSSs compared with usual care or non–AI-based systems in primary care settings. Methods: We conducted a systematic review following the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and reported the results according to PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines. We included experimental and quasi-experimental studies evaluating AI-CDSSs used by health care professionals in primary care settings, compared with usual care or non–AI-based decision support systems, and that reported clinician-, patient-, or system-level outcomes, or safety. An information specialist designed the search strategies and systematically reviewed MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and CENTRAL from inception to June 27, 2025. Reviewers independently performed the selection and extraction processes. Data extraction was informed by the DECIDE-AI and CONSORT-AI (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials–AI) reporting guidelines and the APPRAISE-AI tool. We independently assessed the risk of bias using Risk of Bias-2 or Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of Interventions. Owing to substantial heterogeneity, we conducted a synthesis without meta-analysis and explored heterogeneity using an adapted Non-Adoption, Abandonment, Scale-Up, Spread, and Sustainability–informed implementation-context classification. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251119225). Results: We identified 4074 records through database searches and 12 additional records through citation searching and trial registration checking. We included 14 records on 11 distinct studies, including 4 experimental and 7 quasi-experimental studies. The risk of bias was high in all experimental studies and serious to critical in quasi-experimental studies. AI-CDSSs showed more consistent positive effects on workflow-related outcomes in structured and protocolized decision contexts, particularly for screening, referral, and alert optimization tasks. Patient-level effects were limited and inconsistent, particularly in more complex contexts involving heterogeneous conditions or preference-sensitive decisions. System-level outcomes were heterogeneous, with isolated improvements in service delivery and utilization outcomes. Safety evaluation was rare and poorly specified. Only 2 studies prespecified safety outcomes, and the reported safety information mainly involved technical malfunctions or self-reported side effects. No study reported clinician interaction measures such as agreement with, override of, or reliance on AI outputs. Interpretation of the findings is limited by substantial heterogeneity, short follow-up periods, predominantly high or critical risk of bias, and evidence derived exclusively from high-income countries. Conclusions: AI-CDSSs in primary care may provide more consistent benefits for workflow-related and process-level outcomes in structured and protocolized decision contexts, while evidence on safety remains insufficient to support confident routine implementation. This systematic review reveals an important gap between the rapid development of AI-CDSSs and the lack of robust, comparable evidence to support their reliable use in primary care.
title: AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems in Primary Care: Systematic Review of Clinical Implementation

summary: Background: The rise of video-based social media platforms and the shift toward a video-first content strategy by social media companies have altered how people consume and engage with food-related content. However, little is known about how young adults experience, interpret, and are influenced by food-related videos on social media across different national and cultural contexts. Objective: This paper explores how young adults in Jamaica and the United Kingdom experience, interpret, and are influenced by food-related videos on social media. Methods: Twelve focus groups (online and in-person, 6 in Jamaica and 6 in the United Kingdom) were conducted between August and November 2024. Sixty participants attended the focus groups; after excluding data from 7 individuals suspected of misrepresenting their eligibility, the final dataset included 53 participants aged 18‐25 years. Discussions explored their experiences with food-related videos. Transcripts were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis as the foundation, complemented by framework analysis, and the constant comparison method to facilitate cross-national and cross-cultural comparison. Results: Our analysis generated four themes: (1) young adults balance algorithmic influence with personal curation; (2) young adults engage with food-related videos for relaxation, amusement, and learning; (3) young adults evaluate food-related content through inquiry and strategy—using quick credibility checks such as comparing sources, reviewing comments, assessing transparency, and considering cultural context before deciding whether to trust or ignore content; and (4) food choices form at the intersection of online and offline worlds. A unified high-order theme, “a journey of influence,” captures how young adults move from exposure to evaluation and filter digital experiences through offline realities, leading to change or continuity in dietary attitudes and behaviors. Although this journey was consistent in Jamaica and UK focus groups, the ways young adults interpreted food-related content varied culturally. Conclusions: This cross-national qualitative study showcases how and why young adults engage with food-related videos on social media, and how these interactions shape their attitudes and behaviors toward food and nutrition. Our conceptual map visualizes the influence of food-related videos as a dynamic process unfolding across digital and offline environments, identifying 3 decision points for intervention: exposure, evaluation, and contextualization. These findings highlight opportunities to design youth-responsive digital nutrition interventions that recognize young adults’ agency and the sociocultural and material realities that shape their food choices and eating habits.
title: Engagement and Influence of Food-Related Videos on Social Media Within the Dietary Realities of Young Adults in Jamaica and the United Kingdom: Qualitative Cross-National Study

summary: Background: Conventional triage relies on clinician judgment and limited information available at first contact. AI and machine learning (ML) may improve early risk stratification, whereas tele-triage and patient-facing tools primarily support remote assessment, access, and care routing. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic and prognostic performance of AI- and ML-assisted triage systems and summarize evidence on tele-triage, workflow, implementation, economic, and equity outcomes. Methods: Comparative studies published between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2025, evaluating AI-, ML-, natural language processing–, telehealth-, or digitally enhanced triage. At first, clinical contacts were included. PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, preprint servers, trial registries, and conference proceedings were searched. Screening and data extraction were performed independently in duplicate. Risk of bias was assessed using design-appropriate tools. Clinically comparable area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) estimates were synthesized using random-effects meta-analysis; heterogeneous diagnostic, operational, implementation, economic, and equity outcomes were summarized narratively. Exploratory scenario modeling projected effects per 10,000 emergency department (ED) visits. Results: Twenty-seven studies were included, comprising 13 studies in the quantitative evidence stream and 14 in the narrative synthesis. Four adult ED studies evaluating critical care or deterioration outcomes demonstrated high pooled discrimination for AI-assisted triage (AUC 0.874; 95% CI 0.845‐0.898; ²=94.4%; 95% prediction interval 0.803‐0.922). Four studies reported directly extractable within-study comparisons favoring AI-assisted models (AUC differences of 0.097, 0.120, 0.108, and 0.065), although these could not be pooled because paired variance estimates were unavailable. Admission/disposition studies reported AI-model AUCs ranging from 0.80 to 0.93 and were summarized descriptively because extreme heterogeneity precluded meaningful pooling. Two pediatric studies (AUCs of 0.85‐0.99) were summarized descriptively. Prediction-model studies were primarily limited by deficiencies in model analysis, calibration reporting, and external validation. Narrative evidence suggested improved front-door operational metrics with tele-triage, including reported reductions of 15%‐40% in time to clinical assessment and 2‐8 percentage points in left-without-being-seen rates, whereas patient-facing symptom checkers generally favored sensitivity over specificity. Exploratory scenario modeling illustrated that, under specified prevalence and threshold assumptions, AI-assisted triage could be associated with 12‐38 fewer missed critical illness cases and 45‐120 additional false-positive escalations per 10,000 ED visits. Economic and equity findings were assumption-dependent projections rather than observed clinical, cost-effectiveness, or equity outcomes. Conclusions: AI- and ML-assisted triage models demonstrate promising discrimination for adult ED risk stratification; however, AUC-based discrimination does not establish superiority at clinically relevant decision thresholds, improved patient outcomes, or readiness for clinical implementation. Interpretation is limited by substantial heterogeneity, incomplete threshold-level performance and calibration reporting, limited external validation, and sparse pediatric evidence. Prospective multicenter validation, workflow assessment, subgroup calibration and equity auditing, and formal economic evaluation are required before routine implementation. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251160796; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251160796
title: Technological Integration in Triage With AI and Machine Learning Compared With Conventional Triage and Narrative Synthesis of Telehealth for Patient Prioritization in Emergency and Acute Care Settings: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Video consultations have become an established component of general practice and are increasingly promoted to improve access, efficiency, and health care sustainability. While previous research has primarily explored the perspectives of individual patients and health care professionals, less is known about how organizations involved in strategic video consultation implementation consider their benefits, challenges, and future role within health care systems. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aims to explore the experiences of organizational interest-holders involved in implementing video consultations in Danish general practice, focusing on the perceived strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats related to their use. <strong>Methods:</strong> A qualitative interview study was conducted with 17 representatives from 13 organizations involved in the development, support, regulation, governance, or strategic implementation of video consultations in Denmark. Purposive and snowball sampling identified participants from 4 different organizational groups: patient organizations, professional interest organizations, technology and digital health organizations, and public health authorities. Semistructured interviews were conducted between October and December 2023. Two researchers analyzed the transcripts using a 5-stage deductive-inductive framework analysis. Interest-holder theory defined whose role-informed perspectives were compared; the Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT) analysis framework structured the initial descriptive charting; and iterative comparisons across SWOT categories, organizational groups, and 5 analytical levels identified patterns of convergence, divergence, and tension. <strong>Results:</strong> Four overarching tensions, competing values, and dilemmas emerged across the organizational interest-holder groups: (1) improved access versus widening inequity, (2) efficiency versus relational and clinical quality and safety, (3) digital transformation versus implementation uncertainty, and (4) strategic governance versus target-driven digitalization. Participants recognized that video consultations may improve accessibility, convenience, and coordination of care while supporting broader digital transformation. However, concerns were raised regarding digital exclusion, limitations in relational and clinical assessment, uncertainty about appropriate use, cross-sector implementation challenges, and governance approaches that prioritize use targets over clinical value, quality, and patient safety. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Exploring the perspectives of organizational interest-holders suggested that implementing video consultations in general practice is not simply a matter of increasing technology uptake. Rather, it requires balancing competing priorities related to access and equity, efficiency and quality and safety, digital transformation and implementation uncertainty, and governance and professional autonomy. Sustainable implementation should promote equitable access, context-sensitive clinical use, interoperable digital infrastructure, and good governance. This should be based on research that assesses when video consultations add value, for whom, and according to which definitions of quality and safety, rather than prioritizing uptake alone.
title: Strategic Considerations for Video Consultation Implementation in General Practice: Qualitative Study of Organizational Interest-Holders’ Perspectives
